subject: Agriculture
title: Commodity Trading
description: A short lesson to help you apply Commodity Trading.

hook.text: Four companies—ABCD—control 70% of global grain trade. Most people have never heard of them.

buildup.text: Archer Daniels Midland, Bunge, Cargill, and Louis Dreyfus buy, store, and ship grain across continents.

discovery.text: These traders profit from volatility. When prices spike, traders make money while consumers and farmers suffer.

twist.text: Cargill is privately held—it discloses less financial information than most public companies despite enormous influence.

climax.text: During the 2008 food crisis, commodity speculation drove prices up 80%. Traders profited; 100 million more went hungry.

punchline.text: The companies that feed the world are the ones you've never heard of.

quiz.question: What percentage of global grain trade do the ABCD companies control?

details.summary: Commodity trading buys and sells raw agricultural goods like wheat, corn, and coffee on global exchanges. This topic covers futures markets, price discovery, speculation, and how commodity trading links farmers to consumers across continents.
details.whyItMatters: Commodity prices set at exchanges in Chicago and London determine what billions of people pay for food. Understanding these markets reveals why food prices spike and who profits from volatility.
takeaways: Futures contracts let farmers lock in prices before harvest, reducing risk
Speculators provide market liquidity but can amplify price swings
Four multinational firms—ABCD—control roughly 70% of global grain trade

faq.question: How does agricultural commodity trading work?
faq.answer: Farmers and buyers trade standardized contracts for grain, oilseeds, and other crops on exchanges. Futures contracts set prices for delivery at a future date, allowing both producers and processors to hedge against price uncertainty.

faq.question: Why do food commodity prices fluctuate so much?
faq.answer: Prices respond to weather events, harvest forecasts, export bans, currency shifts, energy costs, and speculative trading. Because supply is seasonal but demand is constant, even small production shortfalls can trigger large price swings.
